questions.prompt: A category manager gives you a flat 'sounds fine' after you present your Q4 proposal. Your instinct is to:

options.text: Move straight to next steps and lock in the booking
Add another data point to strengthen the case
Say thanks and check in again next week
Reflect it back: 'Sounds fine?' and wait
Name what you sense: 'That landed a bit flatter than I expected, what's going on?'

questions.prompt: A brand's trade marketing lead says their last retail media campaign 'didn't work.' Your first move is:

options.text: Reassure them: 'This time will be different, I promise.'
Offer a discount on the next campaign to rebuild goodwill
Ask: 'Can you tell me more about what happened?'
Reflect their words back: 'Didn't work?' and hold the silence
Name the feeling underneath it: 'That result left you wary of trying again.'

questions.prompt: Halfway through a category brief call, the buyer's answers get shorter and shorter. You:

options.text: Speed up to get through the remaining questions
Fill the gap with more detail about your offering
Ask a clarifying question about the brief
Slow down and ask what's changed in the last few minutes
Name it directly: 'You've gone quieter, has something shifted?'

questions.prompt: A category manager says yes to your proposal unusually quickly. You:

options.text: Take the win and move to paperwork
Thank them and confirm the next steps
Ask if there's anything they'd like adjusted before locking it in
Ask what made the decision easy this time
Name what you notice: 'That was faster than I expected, what's driving the urgency?'

questions.prompt: An agency planner keeps steering the conversation back to CPM every time you mention a category insight. You:

options.text: Keep presenting the insight until it lands
Switch entirely to CPM and drop the insight angle
Ask if CPM is the priority for this brief
Ask what's driving the focus on CPM specifically
Name it: 'It feels like CPM is standing in for a bigger concern, is that fair?'

questions.prompt: A buyer agrees to the plan on a video call, but something in their manner doesn't match their words. You:

options.text: Take the verbal agreement and move on
Send a written recap to confirm it in writing
Ask if they have any final questions
Ask gently if everything sits right with them
Name the mismatch: 'You said yes, but something feels unresolved.'

questions.prompt: A trade lead raises their voice slightly when the rate card comes up. You:

options.text: Match their energy to show you're engaged
Go quiet and let them finish
Acknowledge the frustration and keep going
Lower your own voice and slow your pace
Name the shift: 'I can hear this has hit a nerve, let's slow down.'

questions.prompt: You're frustrated after a category manager cancels a call for the third time. Before the reschedule, you:

options.text: Send a slightly terse message noting the cancellations
Say nothing and just rebook
Take a short break before writing back
Notice your own frustration and set it aside before replying
Name it to yourself first, then reply from a clear head

questions.prompt: On a call with both an agency planner and a trade lead, you sense unspoken tension between them. You:

options.text: Address each of them separately after the call
Keep the meeting moving and ignore it
Ask if everyone's aligned before continuing
Slow the pace and watch how they respond to each other
Name it in the room: 'I'm sensing two different priorities here, worth naming?'

questions.prompt: A category manager seems more enthusiastic than the numbers justify. You:

options.text: Match their enthusiasm and move to close
Present the numbers plainly and let them draw conclusions
Ask what's exciting them about the plan
Notice the gap and ask what's really driving the enthusiasm
Name it: 'You sound more excited than the numbers alone explain, what's the real driver?'

questions.prompt: Mid-negotiation, you feel your own patience running thin. You:

options.text: Push to close before it gets worse
Keep talking to fill the silence
Take a breath and keep your tone steady
Notice the feeling and consciously slow your pace
Name it internally, then choose your next words deliberately

questions.prompt: A supplier's trade lead goes unusually quiet after you mention a competing network. You:

options.text: Keep talking through the silence
Change the subject to ease the tension
Ask if they have any thoughts
Sit with the silence and watch for what comes next
Name it: 'That landed differently than I expected, what's on your mind?'

questions.prompt: A category director says your rate card is above every competing network's. You:

options.text: Offer an immediate discount to keep the deal moving
Explain in detail why the number is justified
Ask which competitor they're comparing to
Ask what number would make this an easy yes
Ask what would need to be true for the higher rate to be worth it

questions.prompt: A brand pushes back hard on your incrementality numbers in front of their CFO. You:

options.text: Concede the number may be off to keep the room calm
Defend the methodology at length
Offer to follow up with more detail after the call
Ask what result would satisfy them the number is real
Hold your position and ask them to walk through their own model first

questions.prompt: With two weeks left in the financial year, a client demands a heavy discount to use up budget. You:

options.text: Agree to the discount to secure the spend
Explain why the rate card doesn't flex
Offer a smaller concession to move things along
Offer a value-add instead of a price cut
Hold the price and let the silence sit

questions.prompt: You've just missed a quarterly target. Walking into your next pitch, you:

options.text: Over-explain the miss before getting to the pitch
Avoid mentioning it and hope it doesn't come up
Briefly note it and move on
Mention it plainly and pivot to the plan ahead
Run the pitch exactly as you would if the target had been hit

questions.prompt: A category manager casually mentions they're 'also talking to a competing network.' You:

options.text: Immediately offer better terms to stay competitive
Ignore the comment and continue the pitch
Acknowledge it and keep going
Ask what's drawing them to look elsewhere
Ask what a good outcome from that comparison would look like for them

questions.prompt: A proposal you were confident about gets rejected outright. Your next move is:

options.text: Immediately re-pitch a discounted version
Ask what went wrong in detail
Thank them for the feedback and step back
Let the rejection sit before deciding on a next step
Ask what would need to change for this to be reconsidered later

questions.prompt: You're asked to explain a campaign's results to a category buyer who wasn't across the detail. You:

options.text: Send the full performance deck
List the key metrics: reach, CPM, conversion
Summarise the top three numbers verbally
Frame it as a before-and-after for the category
Tell it as a story: what the brand feared, and what changed for them

questions.prompt: A brand asks why retail media costs more than social. Your answer leads with:

options.text: A straight comparison of CPMs
A list of platform features
A quick explanation of purchase-intent data
A specific before-and-after example from a similar brand
A story about a sceptical brand that changed their mind, and why

questions.prompt: Presenting quarterly results to a room that includes a CFO, you open with:

options.text: The full data table
A summary of every metric tracked
The headline number first
The headline number plus what it meant commercially
A single memorable line the room will repeat afterward

questions.prompt: You're pitching an underperforming format (in-store screens) that you believe still has value. You:

options.text: Present the raw dwell-time data
List the technical specs of the format
Compare it to a similar competitor format
Walk through one campaign where it worked and why
Build the pitch around a moment: the shopper who stopped, looked, and bought

questions.prompt: Wrapping up a strong QBR, your closing line is:

options.text: 'Thanks for your time today.'
'Let's touch base again next quarter.'
A recap of the top three results
A recap plus what it means for next quarter
One sentence built to be repeated to their boss

questions.prompt: A junior category manager needs to relay your pitch to their director, who wasn't on the call. You:

options.text: Send the full slide deck for them to forward
Offer to join the follow-up call yourself
Write a short summary email
Give them three bullet points they can repeat confidently
Hand them a single line built to survive being retold secondhand

questions.prompt: A category manager goes quiet after being your most responsive contact for months. Your gut says:

options.text: They're probably just busy, keep following up on schedule
Something changed internally, dig in before assuming anything
The deal's cooling, move focus elsewhere
Name what you sense: 'The timing may have shifted, I want to respect that.'
Send a breakup message: 'I don't want to keep bugging you.'

questions.prompt: An agency planner suddenly gets much more formal in their emails. You:

options.text: Match the formality and carry on as normal
Ask directly if something's changed
Assume it's just their style and ignore it
Name it gently on the next call
Wait and see if it continues before reacting

questions.prompt: A trade lead who was enthusiastic last quarter seems flat this quarter. You:

options.text: Push the same pitch style that worked before
Ask what's changed since last quarter
Assume budget is tight and move on
Name the shift directly and ask about it
Wait for them to raise it themselves

questions.prompt: A category manager over-praises a mediocre campaign result. You:

options.text: Accept the praise and move to the next pitch
Gently probe what's really landing well for them
Assume they're just being polite
Name the gap: 'That's generous, given the numbers, what's really working for you?'
Say thank you and let it go

questions.prompt: A brand's CFO joins a call unannounced partway through. You:

options.text: Continue exactly as planned
Pause and read the room before continuing
Speed up to finish before they ask questions
Acknowledge them and ask what's most useful for them to hear
Wait for them to speak first

questions.prompt: You sense a category manager is under pressure from their own leadership, though they haven't said so. You:

options.text: Stick to the agenda as planned
Gently ask how things are going on their side
Assume it's not your concern
Name it: 'You seem stretched at the moment, is now still a good time?'
Wait for them to bring it up

questions.prompt: A long-quiet client suddenly books a call with no agenda given. Your gut says:

options.text: It's probably a routine catch-up
Something's changed, prepare for a few scenarios
It's probably bad news, brace for it
Go in curious and ask directly what prompted the call
Wait to see how the call opens before reacting

questions.prompt: EQ Identity EQ1

options.text: When a buyer is emotional, my strength is staying calm and not reacting
My strength is using their emotion as information to guide my next move
My strength is noticing the emotion before they've said anything
My strength is naming the emotion out loud, even when it's uncomfortable

questions.prompt: EQ Identity EQ2

options.text: Under pressure I stay logical and don't let feelings cloud my judgement
Under pressure I look for the emotional lever the other person hasn't used yet
Under pressure, I watch and wait, reading the room before I act
Under pressure, I call out what's really happening, even if it's awkward

questions.prompt: EQ Identity EQ3

options.text: After a difficult meeting I debrief by reviewing what logic/data I used
After a difficult meeting I debrief by thinking about what emotional leverage I did or didn't use
After a difficult meeting, I replay what I noticed: body language, silence, energy
After a difficult meeting I think about whether I named the hard thing or avoided it
